Substantive direct official documents, identified reproductions or indexed source bodies were inspected; source-access limits and action-date decisions are recorded in the review audits. These initial entries do not certify every field.

coverageNotes: A provisional Northwest frontier supplement. No completeness claim; the existence of a discovery listing does not verify all dates or participant identities.
Bounded inventory-first pass, not an exhaustive list. Naval prize cases and privateer logs still contain many unidentified actions.
Capture, recapture, detention, interception, armed combat, and coercive operations are distinct. A prize does not by itself prove an exchange of fire.

Most Navy/Coast Guard histories were inspected through substantial indexed text because direct retrieval returned timeouts, 502, or 403. STCC, Mount Vernon, and Tipton-Haynes pages were retrieved directly.
Dates are preserved at year precision where inconsistent or incomplete. Source summaries are not substitutes for manuscript review.
Only one record is added for an associated action whose unnamed prizes cannot yet be distinguished; aggregate totals are never expanded into invented individual entries.
Adams and John Adams, and several ships named Nancy, Dispatch, La Fortune, and Vengeance, require careful identity control.
Full SC and NC chronology extraction within1776–1782 after removing explicitly known duplicate overview rows, foreign-only incidents, and ambiguous/noncombat items into a candidate queue.
This is a provisional discovery inventory from compiled secondary chronologies. Dates, locations, aliases, participants, and classifications require later verification.
Generic recurring-place numbers are source labels for separate dated incidents; they are retained as aliases/provenance rather than invented battle names.
No casualty totals or copied source narratives were imported.
Indigenous conflicts elsewhere and beyond these lists remain incomplete; additional frontier records follow.
71 additional frontier rows reviewed, including Cherokee, Kentucky, Ohio Valley, and West Virginia actions. This is not a complete accounting.
Classification QA removed false naval matches from the rank Brigadier General and word township; river locations alone are not evidence of naval combat.
Inventory-first extraction; no claim every New Jersey engagement is known.
All dated 1776–1783 entries found in the five alphabetical transcription sections were retained in comprehensive-checklist.json, including context and cross-place aliases.
Provisional locality entries can represent components or duplicate descriptions of one larger action; they are not a verified count of distinct battles.
No casualty/outcome narrative from the compilation is reproduced.
Month-only dates remain YYYY-MM, year-only dates remain YYYY. OCR and the source’s completion-date convention require later checking.

42 additional northern named actions and one NPS Pell’s Point entry supplement the NJ locality inventory. Broad raid/siege records can overlap component actions; parent-child indexing is still required.
DelawareBay1779-12-04 duplicate transcription rows3/4 removed in favorofnamedprizes1/2; other same-date naval entries retained because target descriptions differ.
Incomplete identification pass for overseas, naval, marine landing, privateer, and Revenue Marine actions, 1801–1815. No claim of exhaustive capture coverage.

NHHC direct web retrieval often returned 502; the research pass inspected substantive search-index text of the exact pages. Source-access status records this limitation. NPS full-page text was retrieved.
Names, dates and broad locations are factual inventory fields. Summaries are original and intentionally short; no casualty totals or claimed strategic effects were imported.
Captures and seizures are included but never automatically labeled firefights. Combined raids capturing multiple vessels are grouped when identifiable as one operation.

Several official summaries disagree on dates. Month-only or year-only placement and specific notes preserve uncertainty for Paulina, late-August 1804 bombardments, Nautilus, Rattlesnake, Eagle, Fayal, and Chasseur.
Hundreds of War of 1812 prize captures, additional coastal actions, and Barbary small-craft episodes still need a systematic log/prize-register pass.

Incomplete identification pass for 1801–1815: southern and western U.S.–Indigenous actions, Creek War, Spanish Florida, domestic fighting, and American volunteer participation in the Gutiérrez–Magee expedition.

Purely inter-Creek civil-war actions before direct American participation are retained as context candidates. Creek people fought on several sides; no blanket equation of Creek with Red Stick is intended.

Military captures, seizures, destruction of settlements and supply raids are explicitly labeled operations when combat is not established. Unfought confrontations are context leads rather than battles.
American volunteers in Spanish Texas and Kemper’s West Florida attempt are explicitly unofficial; their inclusion does not assert U.S. Army authorization.

A compilation is discovery provenance, not independent verification. The Eshelman catalogue includes conflicting dates and occasional conflated places. Known problems were reconciled, reduced in precision, or held as candidates.

Fort Mose full-page retrieval failed; indexed excerpts of historical correspondence were inspected. Large Army/Florida PDFs were accessible through indexed excerpts only. Those limits are recorded on relevant records.

Halbert–Ball (1895), Pickett (1851), and Owen (1921) contain period bias and retrospectively collected traditions. Only short original inventory descriptions and factual names/dates/places are extracted. Reported casualty totals and hostile characterizations were not adopted.
Pickett online text declares machine-generated transcription; the scan and contemporary correspondence need comparison before fine details or margin dates become authoritative.
Blackfeet oral histories of Two Medicine are preserved in the discovery note; the common site title is not treated as proof of a conventional battle.
Bounded identification pass for land actions of the War of 1812, plus Tippecanoe and its immediate aftermath in 1811. Not an assertion of complete discovery.
124 records include 7 same-ID enrichments of the starter archive; 117 are additions before cross-batch deduplication.
Dedicated records cover the Detroit/Niagara/St. Lawrence/Champlain fronts, Upper Mississippi, Chesapeake/Potomac, selected Atlantic coast defenses, New Orleans, Fort Bowyer and Fort Peter.

Creek War, Spanish East Florida/Patriot War, Mobile 1813 and Pensacola 1814 were assigned to the frontier batch; ship actions, cutting-out raids and the main Lake Erie/Lake Champlain naval battles were assigned to the naval batch.

61 candidate leads remain outside the counted event inventory. They need original-reference inspection, participant confirmation or de-duplication; several describe multiple contacts that must be split only after verification.

The multi-author 2016 catalogue is a discovery aid, not an infallible authority: it contains contradictory dates, impossible dates such as September 31, obvious 2013/2014 year typos and occasional incorrect state labels.

Month/year precision is intentional for disputed dates, including Campbell's Island, Fort Bowyer's second siege, Tipton's Island and some village raids. Do not silently replace these with January 1 or an arbitrary preferred day.

Fort Meigs and Fort Erie siege records overlap named component actions; parentId and researchNotes disclose the overlap. The west-bank January 8 New Orleans action is a component of the same wider battle.
Indigenous forces appear as independent actors, British allies or U.S. allies as the inspected evidence warrants. Additional nation-specific naming remains necessary.

Further discovery is especially needed for Illinois/Missouri ranger contacts, Fort George picket warfare, village destruction, small Chesapeake raiding actions and New England coastal landing parties. Civilian-only violence is not automatically promoted as U.S. military participation.
Date corrections for Queenston Heights, Thames and Bladensburg are provided explicitly for editorial application. Existing Lundy's Lane, Fort McHenry and New Orleans dates are retained.
1816–1820 bounded expansion covering First Seminole War and selected Gulf/Revenue Marine actions. Coverage remains incomplete.
Dates from contemporary report dates are not silently treated as dates of action. Contradictory day/month claims are explicitly preserved in notes.
Official, tribal and local histories are discovery pointers; full-page retrieval of some government sites was blocked, so indexed passages were inspected.
Unofficial American volunteers are labeled; Indigenous and African participants are identified without treating them as interchangeable.
Single 1801 addendum identified while researching later Texas volunteer history; main frontier-1801-1815 batch remains frozen.
Selected development milestones supplement the engagement inventory. These are institutional events, not battle counts.
Dates follow the cited institutional histories; office establishment, authorization and actual field organization are distinct.
Incomplete identification pass. Captures, recaptures, boat fights, shore raids, and coercive landings are distinguishable action types; this is not a claim that every seizure involved combat.
NHHC and Coast Guard direct retrieval often returned 502 or 403. Exact-page substantive search-index text was inspected where full retrieval failed. Provenance records access mode.
Primary legal documents are used to check contemporary piracy labels. Marianna Flora is a merchant-vessel confrontation; Palmyra, Federal, and Fenix have contested legal classifications.
Dates intentionally retain month or year precision where official or primary accounts conflict. In particular, Siguapa’s July 11 is a report date, not an established action day.
Grouped captures are retained as operations when the sources do not distinguish individual capture encounters. Multiple recovered vessels from one battle are not independently counted as battles.
1829 has no confirmed combat record in this batch. An unsuccessful patrol, a shipwreck, and civilian merchant victims are not used to manufacture military engagements for a sparse year.

Remaining work includes systematic squadron logs, Revenue Marine court records, additional West Indies small-craft operations, African anti-slavery prize papers, and original Aegean correspondence. This batch does not exhaust the decade.

Discovery inventory for land, Indigenous, domestic, and explicitly unofficial American-party actions in 1821–1830. Naval and anti-piracy actions are assigned separately. This batch does not establish completeness.
Every event has an inspected source. Leads based only on indexed excerpts or unresolved chronology are kept in candidates. Listed is the research status, not a claim of full verification.

Private American trapping parties and preannexation Texas colonists are explicitly distinguished from U.S. government forces. Their presence does not turn a Mexican or Indigenous conflict into a federal U.S. war.

Indigenous communities had independent political interests; Native attacks, American-initiated shootings, village destruction, and coercive removals are represented without adopting settler justifications.
No event is manufactured to fill an otherwise sparse year. The absence of an entry is not evidence of peace or a completed search.
Campaign containers, bloodless seizures, coercive operations, and institutional incidents are labeled by category. They must not be added together and described as a count of distinct battles.
Pattie, Beckwourth, and other retrospective narratives require chronological reconciliation. Unsupported or sensational casualty figures were omitted.
Identification-level research batch for 1831–1835 land military actions, focused on the Black Hawk War and the opening of the Second Seminole War. It does not assert exhaustive coverage.
Thirty-eight listed records include two same-ID starter enrichments, leaving thirty-six net additions if those starter IDs are present.
Dates use year, month or day precision honestly. A broad date does not imply continuous fighting; disputed dates remain in researchNotes rather than being silently resolved.

Black Hawk War coverage includes Indigenous participants allied with either side, independent local raiders, attacks on civilians, U.S. coercive actions and pursuit of refugees. A tribal name never implies unanimous national participation.

Army, state militia, territorial militia, federal troops and U.S.-allied Indigenous forces are labeled distinctly. Empty branches arrays mean no U.S. armed-service unit has been established for a civilian-target attack.

Bad Axe retains its existing ID and becomes a two-day massacre-category record, with battle terminology kept in the title and aliases. The label does not deny armed resistance; it identifies the extensive killing of noncombatants.
Prophetstown here is Wabokieshiek’s Illinois village; no duplication of Tenskwatawa’s 1811 Indiana village is intended.
Madison straggler killings are explicitly a component of the Wisconsin Heights approach. No umbrella entry for the entire Black Hawk War is added on top of all its components.
The lower Wisconsin River refugee attacks remain one month-level operation pending separation of gunboat and shore contacts. These Army-directed gunboats are not automatically U.S. Navy actions.
Noncombat military operations—Saukenuk expulsion, detention of mediators, custody transfer, the two dragoon expeditions and Bulow occupation—are operations, not battles.

The single Bulow occupation record crosses into January 1836. Its start is within this batch; independent 1836 events including Dunlawton, Mala Compra’s occupation/destruction, Bulow’s burning, Fort Izard and Gaines’s campaign are reserved for the next period.

Toledo boundary-dispute fighting and military suppression of Nat Turner’s rebellion are included as domestic militia/federal operations. Independent Texas Revolution fighting is assigned to the root researcher and not duplicated here.

Published history, state/tribal/government interpretations, historical artifacts and some secondary identification entries were inspected. All remain researchStatus listed; this is not full fact-check certification.

Some official sources contain errors or outdated interpretations. The Army CMH campaign-summary claim of 330 men in Dade’s column and the Illinois Archives August 3 Bad Axe date are not adopted. Casualty totals, rhetorical language and questionable tribal attributions are generally omitted.

Unpromoted candidates include ambiguous civilian incidents, unresolved sub-actions and rejected legends. Candidate lists are not event counts, and generic source-discovery links do not verify those candidates.
Direct fetches of some historical PDFs returned 403/timeouts. inventorySources explicitly distinguishes inspected indexed passages from full-text reads.
Selected 1831–1835 naval/Marine operations, not a complete list. Protecting residents and coercive landings are kept distinct from established combat.
The proposed 1835 São Tomé expedition was not executed according to the inspected USNI account; it was not added as a battle.
Falklands terminology, jurisdiction and piracy allegations remain contested rather than resolved by a U.S. naval label.
Supplementary pre-annexation Texas and American-volunteer records are explicitly labeled. They are not U.S. federal military operations.
Béxar campaign records overlap dated components; seizure without fire, battle and execution are distinguished.
Doubtful exact days are reduced to month precision; no casualty totals or copied narratives are imported.
Systematic 1812 privateer catalogue discovery queue added separately from engagement records. The queue has not passed action-by-action verification.
Source warns that capture/report dates, vessel aliases and duplicate prizes are unresolved; some listed years are demonstrably suspect. Those issues are flagged rather than silently promoted.
Aggregate cruise totals and unnamed targets remain single leads. No capture or ransom is automatically represented as a firefight.
Existing IDs are preserved when researched corrections refine names, territorial geography, participation or classification. The previous values and evidence remain in metadataRevision.
Separate addendum to the frozen blackhawk-1831-1835 batch, following the root researcher’s explicit inclusion of organized unofficial trapping-party actions.
Ten listed records; no claim of exhaustive fur-trade coverage. All branches identify organized armed civilians, not U.S. regular forces.
Pierre’s Hole (1832) and Fort McKenzie (1833) include Indigenous combatants and civilian-target violence; neither is silently labeled a United States Army battle.
The June 1835 Pierre’s Hole camp fight is a different event from July 1832. The Fort McKenzie illustration’s production date is not its event date.
The journals contain 1836–1843 contacts as well; those were not backdated into 1831–1835.
Titles for small incidents are descriptive indexing labels where no standard battle name was established.
Original participant accounts remain culturally and politically situated; attacker labels, casualties and motives need further comparison.
Supplementary Texas Revolution and local armed-party inventory, with explicit pre-annexation force labels. U.S. Navy enforcement is separately identified.
Sieges, operations and dated component actions overlap. They must not be summed as independent verified battles.
Prisoner executions, settler raids, unopposed seizures and military captures are distinguished from established exchanges of fire.
Domestic militia actions, organized unofficial American incursions into Canada, and coercive operations are separately labeled. Inclusion does not imply federal authorization.
Noncombat mobilizations and failed seizures remain operations, not invented battles. Civilian election brawls and uncorroborated raids remain research candidates.
Missouri and Illinois accounts should be researched using state records, participant accounts and scholarship from multiple communities.
Western coverage explicitly includes provisional and territorial volunteers, settler militia and organized private armed parties. These are not automatically U.S. Regular Army actions.
Cayuse, Pomo, Diné and Timpanogos community perspectives and victim status need sustained research. Historical collective-guilt and triumphalist battle labels are not adopted as conclusions.
Campaign and retreat containers overlap component contacts. Broad sources support discovery only; no exhaustive claim or casualty aggregate is made.
Selected institutional milestones supplement the action directory. Authorization, opening, organization and subsequent renaming are distinct dates; development entries are not battle totals.
California documentary-appendix leads preserve small Army, auxiliary and organized settler attacks for follow-up. These are unresolved leads rather than promoted engagements.

Underlying participant accounts, Indigenous testimony and newspaper reports remain to be inspected. Reported death estimates are deliberately not imported. Some catalogue rows are alternative accounts of one incident.
Frozen inventory batch after source and structural review. It is a substantial first pass, not a claim of complete coverage.

Inventory of land, Indigenous, domestic, removal, and explicitly unofficial American-party actions in 1836–1845. Naval Florida operations are included by agreement; overseas naval and Mexican War actions are assigned separately.

Records include campaign containers and coercive operations as well as battles. Their total is not a count of distinct battles. Treaty negotiations without armed coercion are not automatically engagements.

Sprague’s 1848 book contains official contemporary reports but reflects Army and settler perspectives. Its racial descriptions, claims about motives, and most casualty estimates are not adopted. OCR dates must be checked against other evidence.

Republic of Texas actions are explicitly distinguished from U.S. federal operations. Unofficial American-connected fur-trade and Mexican Federalist parties are labeled as such; unrelated intertribal wars and unverified isolated murders are not automatically included.

Important unresolved leads remain in 1836–1839 Florida, coastal canoe operations, north Florida and Georgia, and Texas local actions. The absence of a listed event in 1845 does not establish that no military action occurred.
Canadian Patriot War, Missouri Mormon War, Dorr Rebellion, Toledo, and other domestic additions are handled in a separate coordinated batch.

Identification inventory, not a claim of exhaustive coverage or completed historical review. Sources identify events and expose date disagreements; detailed narratives and wider source comparison remain pending.

Scope: naval and Marine overseas actions, armed landings, coercive seizures and anti-slave-trade captures, plus naval operations against Mexican ports. Second Seminole War Navy/Marine inland operations are assigned to the frontier batch; Mexican Army land battles and California/Baja volunteer battles are assigned to the land batch.

Operations explicitly described as unopposed, detention, or seizure are not represented as proven gun battles. Later judicial release is preserved. Military transport, patrol, port visits, diplomatic salutes and local Liberian militia actions are not automatically American engagements.

Month or year precision is deliberate where original reports disagree or exact dates remain unverified. In particular: Pons November 30/December 1, 1845; Chancellor 1846/1847 table discrepancy; Admittance April 7/8, 1847; La Paz April 13/14; Creole November 20/26, 1846; Martha June 6/7, 1850.

The United States Exploring Expedition’s coercive actions are described without adopting the racialized or one-sided framing of nineteenth-century reports. Fijian, Samoan and I-Kiribati accounts remain an important next research layer.
The entire 1836–1850 span is represented by the inventory scope, but sparse years are not padded with routine duties. Candidates remain outside the event count.

Primary sources inspected include Wilkes’s original narratives and dated orders, Perry’s December 1843 correspondence, Jamestown’s log transcription, Supreme Court case statements, congressional capture tables, and participant accounts of Mexican naval operations. Some NHHC and government PDFs were read through substantive indexed text when direct retrieval failed.
No existing starter IDs overlap this batch at the time of the initial read; land starter records for Monterrey, Veracruz and other Army battles are intentionally left to the land batch.
All forces are explicitly the preannexation Republic of Texas Navy, not the United States Navy. This geographic-predecessor supplement must not be presented as U.S. federal military combat.

Parent owns 1836 Texas naval actions, including Warren’s seizure of Invincible; no duplication is included here. Storm losses, shipbuilding, ordinary patrols and later executions are context rather than engagements.

Thompson’s August29, 1837 report explicitly says detailed papers were destroyed in the wreck. Year-only dates for earlier cruise contacts are intentional. Two different Correo captures are separately dated in his report, while unclear spellings and aggregate prize names remain candidates.

The 1837 Sisal location and August27 Galveston action follow the contemporary report rather than conflicting later summaries. The April 30 and May 16, 1843 Campeche battles follow Walke’s actual journal. Unresolved surgeon-caption dates do not create a third battle.
Coercive seizures and landings are operations; no gunfire is inferred from a prize alone. Little Penn attribution and neutral-vessel claims are stated with their uncertainty.
Coverage is identification-stage and incomplete, with sparse years preserved. Full source comparison and Mexican/Yucatecan evidence remain next research layers.

Identification inventory, not an exhaustive claim or final narrative. Covers 1846–1848 land actions against Mexico, resistance in occupied New Mexico, California, and Army/volunteer actions in Baja California. Frémont’s attacks on Native communities and Doniphan’s Navajo expedition are explicitly separate conflicts.

The coordinated naval batch owns port landings, initial California naval occupations including Los Angeles August 13, Sonoma July 9, Bartlett’s December 8 capture, San José/San Vicente garrison and relief actions, Mulegé, Guaymas, Mazatlán/Urias, Tabasco, Alvarado and Tuxpan. Those records are not duplicated here.
Five starter IDs are retained and dateCorrections supplied: Palo Alto, Monterrey, Buena Vista, Veracruz and Chapultepec.

Operation includes armed standoffs, bloodless occupations, rescues, captures and composite pursuits. These are not all battles. Parent/component overlap is identified; the total is a record count, not an independent battle count.

Native, Hispano, Californio and Mexican resistance is identified without adopting derogatory language from contemporary reports. Civilian and prisoner killings are distinguished from conventional battles. Empty branches indicate civilian victims rather than invented Army units.
YYYY or YYYY-MM reflects supported precision. Notes preserve contested printed dates, report dates, departure versus assault dates and known catalogue errors.

Heitman is a discovery index with demonstrable errors, including Sacramento placed in California, Palo AltoMay 18, Todos SantosApril 30 and conflicting Rosales/Zacualtipán dates. Unresolved catalogue names remain candidates; aliases are not additional battles.

Lally’s four August actions are separate contacts. Tolomé/Paso de Ovejas and June La Hoya fighting remain composites pending report reconciliation. Original War Department convoy reports, unit returns and Mexican archives are priority follow-ups.
Institutional developments and treaties are not counted as engagements. The Navajo expedition is an operation without invented component battles.

Known gaps include other 1846–1848 U.S.–Indigenous frontier actions, escorts and private expeditions, unidentified guerrilla attacks, occupation atrocities, and the unresolved catalogue leads. This batch does not establish complete coverage.

Bounded sweep of Heitman volumeII printed page400, cross-checked against alphabetical and officer-casualty entries, plus limited independent corroboration. Five promoted identification records and fourteen unresolved discovery leads; no claim of completeness.

Cayuse War, Battle Creek, Fort Utah, Washington’s Navajo expedition, Narbona and Bloody Island belong to the parent batch and are excluded here. Heitman’s May 9, 1850 Clear Lake and Pitt River combined label is not promoted as a new battle date.

The extracted page is arranged in columns, so catalogue unit attributions in candidates remain provisional until visual page/report comparison. Alphabetical and casualty entries from the same book are internal consistency checks, not independent sources.

Alias clusters prevent duplicate inflation: Frio Pass/Leona and possible Lavaca; Inge/Duncan; Nueces/Rio Grande; Too Koon Kurre/Red River; and Costillo/Canadian/Red River. Modern georeferencing remains uncertain for several historical river names.

No Indigenous nation, commander, tactical result or casualty number is invented from a place/date catalogue alone. Promoted Las Vegas record retains the conflicting American and Jicarilla descriptions of the confrontation.

Additional primary-discovery trail: Texas Indian Papers volumeV contains 1850 letters from Hardee and others; National Archives RG393 post and department records provide the route to original Army reports.
Bleeding Kansas and domestic armed operations include official and unofficial parties with explicit labels. Opponents are not reduced to generic domestic-enemy terminology.

Operations include rescues, disarmaments, armed standoffs and coercive escorts; these are not all battles. Indigenous Plains campaigns are coordinated in a separate batch even where they occur within Kansas.

Participant letters and later reminiscences can be partisan and chronologically imperfect. Named-action discovery precedes detailed review; individual political killings and ordinary riots remain scope-review leads.
California coverage includes state-sanctioned and independent armed forces, Army detachments, forced removals and community massacres. It is not complete.
Tolowa, Wiyot and other community accounts are essential; all sources can have chronology errors. Conflicting years are explicit and are not multiplied into separate events.
Northern California research remains especially incomplete at the village and detachment level. Documentary timeline entries are often report dates; unresolved details stay candidates.

Filibuster expeditions are explicitly unofficial American-connected forces, often serving in local or multinational armies. Their inclusion does not imply federal authorization or classify entire foreign countries as U.S. belligerents.
Central American and Mexican sources accompany the expedition leader’s self-justifying narrative. Motive claims, racial terminology and casualty estimates are not adopted.
Campaign containers, sieges and individual assaults overlap. Lesser contacts, naval seizures, prisoner executions and unclear expedition plans remain candidates until distinguishable.
Selected1850s military-development milestones accompany the engagement directory; authorization, organization and implementation dates are distinguished.
Frozen bounded inventory, 1851–1860: Plains, Southwest and Utah land contacts, including Yuma/Mojave/Paiute border conflicts and Cheyenne contacts in Kansas. It is not a complete list of the decade.
Northern and central California, Pacific Northwest/Idaho/eastern Oregon, Florida, Bleeding Kansas partisan violence and overseas naval actions are assigned to other batches.
All records remain researchStatus listed. A source inspection establishes a usable identification, not a completed multi-perspective historical account.

Civilian and territorial-militia contacts are explicitly labeled in branches; none is silently represented as a regular United States Army battle. Empty branches identify civilian victims where a service attribution would mislead.

Broad military operations are labeled operation and have overlap notes. The Navajo expedition of 1851, Yuma campaign, Echo Canyon defenses and Carleton punitive campaign are not additive battle counts.

Multiple dates or place names in a catalogue do not automatically produce multiple records. Penasco, White Mountains, Santa Catarina, Witherell’s West Nueces contact, the Utah wagon burnings, Williams Station and several January 1860 scouts retain date uncertainty.

The source cache includes Heitman volume II, Brackett 1865, Price 1883, five regimental histories, Fort Union chapter 3 and the NPS Joshua Tree Mojave ethnography. Many smaller Heitman identities remain explicit candidates for the next pass.
Native participants and civilian losses are retained in titles, summaries and notes. Older sources contain racial language and Army self-justifications which are not adopted as factual assessments.

Important gaps include the individual 1852 Quechan punitive raids, all Walker/Tintic militia contacts, the minor 1858–1860 Navajo campaign contacts, individual 1860 Pony Express station raids, Texas Rangers’ small contacts and further civilian camp attacks. No quiet year is treated as proof that no actions occurred.
FROZEN for parent integration after bounded source, date, schema, duplicate, and scope review.
Pacific Northwest, joint coastal, Snake/Idaho, and Florida actions in 1851–1860. Other agents cover California, Plains/Southwest/Utah, and domestic/Kansas.

Campaigns, destruction raids, forced removals, and armed occupations are identified as operations, not additional pitched battles. Named actions may be grouped when the source does not distinguish their dates.
The Siletz-hosted timeline is a source discovery document credited to University of Washington Press. Thin entries retain explicit unit/date limits and do not claim detailed verification.

Cross-border exceptions were coordinated with root: Ben Wright and Bloody Point in the Modoc homeland, and unofficial American miner actions in British Columbia. American participants are not automatically federal soldiers.
Dates remain approximate when records conflict. No battle or absence of fighting is invented for a year with sparse coverage. Heitman-only minor contacts generally remain candidates.

The source-linked inventory is not exhaustive. Indigenous community histories, archaeological research, contemporary military reports, and state/federal histories sometimes conflict; notes preserve consequential differences.

Identification pass, not a complete census or finished narrative history. Listed means a specific named action or substantial armed operation is documented; it does not mean every detail or interpretation has been verified.

Includes federal Navy and Marine actions overseas, armed protective landings, coercive naval demonstrations, named suspected-slaver seizures, and specified domestic Marine operations. Naval captures are not automatically gun battles.

This naval inventory covers federal enforcement and protection. Pacific Northwest joint coastal actions, Florida boat operations, Army frontier actions and unofficial American filibuster battles are addressed separately in the broader directory.

Harpers Ferry raid/local fighting and the federal Marine assault are connected separately dated entries. Christiana Marine arrest assistance is separate from the September11 civilian/marshal clash in the parent batch.

No invented day dates for source disagreements, no named captures derived only from aggregate totals, and no expansion of unnamed junks or villages into fictitious individual events. Sources retain historical prejudices and U.S. officials’ justificatory claims; summaries do not adopt those as neutral descriptions.

Material catalogue/date errors documented: Koszta1853 not1849; Waya1858 not1859; Jaffa1858–59 not1851; Kissembo renewed landingMarch3vs4; RachelBrownJanuaryvsFebruary1853; GambrillNovembervsDecember1853; DeliciaDecember21vsSeptember21; WildfireApril26vs28; CoraSeptember25vs26. Sparse years remain open.
The1859 and1860 Navy annual reports were downloaded and locally extracted for source review; cached text is a research aid and may contain OCR errors. Original PDF pages remain the citation targets.

FROZEN inventory pass: 354 land/coastal principal records, comprising 353 entries from the inspected technical-volume code list and the later AR018 resurvey addition. Twelve preserve existing starter IDs; eight explicit date corrections refine year-only starters. Existing indexed statuses are preserved; new records are listed, not fully researched.

This is a systematic principal-battlefield catalogue inventory, not a complete inventory of Civil War engagements. Skirmishes, raids, guerrilla attacks, naval contacts, seizures, civilian massacres, and campaign components extend far beyond this catalogue and require separate discovery.

The downloaded technical volume yields 383 individually coded entries. A commonly used 384-row derivative includes combined VA020 as well as VA020A and VA020B. This batch counts the two described engagements and omits the combined study-area umbrella; it does not assert the original commission’s headline 384-site count is wrong.

Thirty technical-volume codes are delegated: 21 naval, two Minnesota frontier, and seven later frontier/massacre sites. catalogueCoverage enumerates all 383 codes and owners. These are deliberate assignments, not silent omissions; combined coverage must be audited before publication.

Army in branches denotes the United States/Union Army in this conflict; Confederate Army is separately labelled. Home guards, secessionist state guard/militia, Confederate guerrillas, Union-aligned Indigenous forces, and civilian victims are distinguished where the principal action was not a regular federal Army encounter.

Navy is included for identified mixed land/coastal actions. This is participation labelling, not a claim to enumerate every supporting vessel or Confederate service. Marine Corps participation is explicit at First Bull Run and the second Fort Fisher attack.

Final cross-batch audit added Navy to LA003 Baton Rouge using the technical-volume narrative on PDF page 50; August 5 gunboat support and August 6 destruction of CSS Arkansas are distinct dated contacts.

Date precision follows the inspected printed catalogue Date(s) field, crosschecked against the attributed structured transcription, except documented GA003 year correction and retained precise baseline combat dates for SC001/MD003. Broad catalogue intervals can include approach, siege, withdrawal, or occupation; they are not automatically continuous fighting dates.

Current NPS CWSS battle-detail Date(s) fields sometimes show campaign dates rather than engagement dates. They are not used mechanically to replace the technical-volume dates. Narratives, edition differences, apparent errors, and overlapping principal operations need continued review.

Aliases are discovery aids, not additional events. Generic repeated names refer to distinct dated engagements when their CWSAC codes differ. Campaign umbrellas and components remain explicitly noted; site totals should not be presented as counts of independent non-overlapping combat actions.

The supplied summaries are deliberately short inventory descriptions, with no casualty counts or comprehensive outcome narratives. The identification is sourced; full research and source-quality review remain pending.

Arnold, American Civil War Battle Data v11.0.0, https://github.com/jrnold/acw_battle_data, licensed CC BY 4.0 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Selection, formatting, brief summaries, source inspection, exception notes, and corrections were added for this inventory; the NPS technical volume is the principal identification source.

Native nations and Black troops were participants across many Union and Confederate formations; this inventory does not pretend that an Army label supplies a complete unit-by-unit or tribal participation roster.

Bounded identification pass for 1861–1862, emphasizing naval fighting, boat raids, military-vessel seizures, armed coastal occupations and a separately named set of Confederate commerce-raiding captures. Not a claim that every naval action or prize is yet identified.

The principal discovery catalogue is the U.S. Navy’s public-domain Civil War Naval Chronology (1966), inspected through four locally cached USNLP transcription pages. Blue submarine additions on that website are not automatically treated as original Navy entries.

NPS Technical Volume II was used to cross-check the delegated principal naval actions. Its conflicts with Navy chronology dates are retained explicitly. Month or year precision is used where the sources do not agree.
